strengths: The paper addresses a clear and relevant limitation of Decision Transformers—limited context length due to quadratic attention complexity—by adapting the Recurrent Memory Transformer (RMT) idea from NLP to offline RL.
The ablation studies are reasonably thorough, examining number of segments, memory size, presence/absence of memory tokens (DT-XL baseline), and segment overlap/memory fixation for MuJoCo.

The attention map visualizations (Figures 7-10) provide some interpretability evidence that memory tokens are actively read from and written to across segments, which is a nice qualitative complement to the quantitative results.
Code and weights are stated to be publicly available, aiding reproducibility.

The comparison against DT-XL (a Transformer-XL-style baseline without explicit memory tokens but with the same segment training) is a good ablation to isolate the specific contribution of the memory mechanism itself.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: the core idea is essentially a direct application of the Recurrent Memory Transformer (RMT) mechanism to the Decision Transformer architecture, with relatively little new methodological insight beyond combining known components (RMT + DT + TransformerXL-style hidden state caching).

The MuJoCo results are weak and inconsistent: RMDT underperforms DT and/or CQL/TAP on several tasks (e.g., HalfCheetah across all settings, Medium-Replay Hopper/Walker2d vs CQL), and the reported standard deviations are very large (e.g., Hopper Medium-Expert 111.0 ± 18.9, Medium-Replay Walker2d 72.1 ± 16.1), making it unclear whether the mean improvements are statistically meaningful. The claim of being 'significantly superior' is not well supported for MuJoCo.

Only 4 Atari games are tested, which is a small and non-standard subset (the original DT paper and most follow-up works test more games); results are not normalized to human/gamer scores, making it harder to compare with prior literature and assess true significance.

Table 1 (Atari) results, while showing improvement, also come with substantial variance overlap in some cases (e.g., Pong 17.1 ± 0.94 vs DT-XL 16.6 ± 0.99), and no statistical significance testing (e.g., t-tests) is reported despite only 3 seeds being used.

The MuJoCo evaluation protocol described (different training regime with three segments, 25% overlap, and memory fixation chosen post hoc via ablation on the test set) raises concerns about hyperparameter selection using the evaluation results themselves, which could bias reported performance.

The related work and background sections are lengthy relative to the core technical contribution, while the method description of the actual training procedure (particularly gradient flow through detached memory, and how loss is computed per segment) could be clearer and more rigorous.

No comparison to other more recent or stronger context-extension baselines (e.g., simply increasing DT's context window naively without memory, or comparing wall-clock/memory efficiency gains) is provided, which would help substantiate the practical benefit of the added architectural complexity.

The paper's central motivating claim—that longer effective context (up to 150 frames) helps—is only weakly supported since Atari and MuJoCo are known to have fairly short-horizon dependencies, and the ablation shows performance saturates or even degrades with more segments/memory size in several environments, undercutting the motivation for the approach.
Limited discussion of computational overhead/training complexity introduced by the segment-based training and memory update procedure compared to vanilla DT baseline.

strengths: The core idea of combining recurrent memory tokens (RMT-style) with Decision Transformer for offline RL is a reasonable and relevant direction given the quadratic-complexity limitations of vanilla transformers in long-horizon RL.
The ablation studies (number of segments, memory size, use of memory tokens vs. DT-XL, segment overlay) are relatively thorough and attempt to isolate the contribution of individual design choices.
The attention-map visualizations for read/write memory subsequences provide some qualitative insight into how the memory tokens are used across segments, which is a nice attempt at interpretability.
Code and weights are stated to be publicly released, which aids reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: Very limited novelty: the method is essentially a direct application of the existing Recurrent Memory Transformer (RMT) mechanism to the existing Decision Transformer framework, with little new technical insight beyond combining these two known components.

The core comparison in Table 1 is confounded: DT-XL (segment-wise training without memory tokens) already produces a massive jump over DT (e.g., Qbert 7830→12300), while RMDT provides only a small additional gain over DT-XL. This suggests that most of the benefit comes from segmented/chunked training rather than the proposed recurrent memory mechanism itself, undermining the central claim of the paper.
Atari evaluation is narrow (only 4 games) due to stated compute constraints, which is insufficient for a top-tier venue given how central the Atari results are to the paper's main claims.

MuJoCo results are weak and inconsistent: RMDT underperforms CQL, DT, and/or TAP on multiple settings (e.g., Medium-Expert HalfCheetah, Medium-Expert Walker2d, Medium-Replay HalfCheetah, Medium-Replay Hopper), and the overall mean score improvement over CQL is negative, while improvement over DT/TAP is marginal (75.2 vs 74.7). This does not support the claim of the method being 'significantly superior' in this domain.

Extremely high variance in MuJoCo results (e.g., Hopper Medium-Expert 111.0 ± 18.9, HalfCheetah Medium-Replay 35.9 ± 11.2) raises concerns about the statistical reliability and robustness of the reported gains; no significance testing is provided.

The paper required substantial hyperparameter tuning specific to MuJoCo (segment overlay percentage, memory fixation) to make the method competitive at all, suggesting sensitivity and lack of robustness/generality of the proposed approach across domains.

The interpretability analysis (attention maps) is purely qualitative and anecdotal (a single randomly selected head/segment), without any quantitative metric to substantiate claims that memory 'effectively encodes' long-range information.

Missing important baselines/comparisons, e.g., no comparison with other long-context RL transformer approaches (e.g., Trajectory Transformer with segment-level memory, or other memory-augmented transformer variants beyond Transformer-XL), limiting the positioning of the contribution relative to prior work discussed in Section 2.

The writing contains several typos/errors (e.g., 'MoJoko' instead of 'MuJoCo', 'he timestep' instead of 'the timestep', ambiguous captions in Figures 9/10 which appear duplicated), reducing overall polish and clarity.

No analysis of computational/memory overhead of RMDT relative to DT or DT-XL, despite the motivation of the paper being to address the quadratic complexity problem — a direct efficiency comparison (e.g., runtime, memory footprint, wall-clock training time) is absent.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: extending Decision Transformer's limited context via recurrent memory mechanisms, analogous to RMT in NLP.

The DT vs DT-XL vs RMDT comparison on Atari is a clean ablation that isolates the specific contribution of memory tokens from simply preserving hidden states/longer context, which is scientifically valuable.
Extensive ablation studies are provided (number of segments, memory embedding size, segment overlay, memory fixation), giving good insight into what design choices matter for RMDT's performance.

The attention-map based memory survey (Section 7) provides a reasonably compelling qualitative/interpretability analysis showing that the memory subsequences are actively read/written in structured ways across segments and layers.
Code and model weights are stated to be publicly released, supporting reproducibility.
Consistent, non-negligible improvements are shown across all four Atari games tested, with reduced variance relative to DT baselines.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the core idea is largely a direct application of the existing Recurrent Memory Transformer (RMT) mechanism to the existing Decision Transformer architecture, without substantial new algorithmic contributions beyond engineering adaptations (segment overlay, memory fixation).

MuJoCo results are mixed and not clearly convincing: RMDT underperforms CQL, DT, or TAP on several settings (e.g., Medium-Expert Walker2d, Medium-Replay HalfCheetah, Medium-Replay Hopper vs CQL), and the overall mean improvement over TAP/DT is marginal while still below CQL, undermining the claim of general superiority.

High variance in MuJoCo results (e.g., ±14-19 for several environments) raises concerns about statistical significance of the reported improvements; no significance testing is reported despite only 3 seeds being used.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only 4 Atari games and 3 MuJoCo tasks are tested, explicitly attributed to limited computational resources, which limits confidence in generalizability of the claimed superiority.

The ablation in Table 3 suggests that much of the MuJoCo performance gain comes from engineering tricks (segment overlay and memory fixation) rather than the memory mechanism itself (RMDT† vs RMDT‡ shows large jumps from overlay alone), which somewhat undercuts the paper's central claim that recurrent memory tokens are the primary driver of improvement.

No comparison to other established memory mechanisms (e.g., Compressive Transformer, Memorizing Transformer) as baselines beyond a self-constructed DT-XL variant, limiting the strength of the comparative claims.

Writing and presentation have rough edges (e.g., typo 'Mojoko' in the abstract, some unclear or inconsistent notation/cross-referencing), which detracts from overall polish expected at a top-tier venue.

The claimed 'interpretable properties' of memory (Section 7) are largely qualitative attention-map visualizations without quantitative or causal validation that memory content is actually responsible for the observed performance gains.

strengths: Addresses a clear and relevant gap: incorporating recurrent memory (RMT-style) into transformer-based offline RL (Decision Transformer), which is a natural and underexplored combination.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning memory-intensive environments (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze) as well as standard benchmarks (Atari, MuJoCo/D4RL), showing the method is not narrowly tuned to one setting.

Thoughtful ablations: curriculum learning necessity for T-Maze, number of segments, memory size, and a RATE- (no-memory) control that isolates the contribution of memory tokens versus segment-wise training alone.
Interpretability analysis via attention maps provides some qualitative evidence that memory tokens are actually being read/written and used across segments, going beyond just aggregate scores.
Code is released publicly, aiding reproducibility.
Qualitative trajectory visualization (Figure 3) on ViZDoom gives an intuitive, convincing illustration of the memory-forgetting phenomenon that motivates the approach.
weaknesses: The T-Maze environment is a non-standard, heavily modified variant of the benchmark used in prior work (Ni et al., 2023), making it harder to compare results to the existing literature and raising questions about whether the setup was tailored to favor RATE.

Gains on Atari and MuJoCo (environments that do not require long memory) are inconsistent: RATE underperforms DT/CQL on several MuJoCo Medium-Replay and Medium settings (e.g., HalfCheetah Medium, Hopper Medium-Replay), undercutting the claim of 'better or comparable' results across the board.

The ablation on memory size (Appendix D.2) shows that increasing memory length does not improve results in 3 of 4 Atari environments, which weakens the core narrative that memory content itself (rather than segment-wise training/curriculum) is driving improvements; the RATE- control helps but the story is still not fully clean (e.g., RATE- already captures much of the gain over DT in Qbert).
Only 3 seeds (Atari/MuJoCo) or moderate seed counts are used, and confidence intervals are often wide (e.g., ViZDoom RATE: 16.46 ± 6.90), making some comparisons only weakly significant.

The novel MuJoCo evaluation protocol (resetting return-to-go at each segment) is a nonstandard modification introduced specifically to make segment-based training work, but its effect on fairness of comparison to DT/CQL/TAP (which use the standard protocol) is not carefully analyzed or ablated.

Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely transplants RMT's read/write memory-token mechanism into the DT framework with modified curriculum training; the core architectural contribution is limited.

Writing quality has issues (e.g., 'memory toxins' typo, awkward phrasing throughout), and some methodological details (e.g., exact curriculum procedure, why weighted-loss alternatives were rejected in favor of curriculum) could be clearer.

Baseline DT hyperparameters/training budgets in ViZDoom/T-Maze are not clearly matched or tuned as carefully as RATE's, raising concerns about fairness of the comparison given RATE's specialized curriculum training was hand-designed for these tasks.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: integrating recurrent memory mechanisms (inspired by RMT) into transformer-based offline RL (Decision Transformer), motivated by the quadratic cost of full self-attention.
Experiments span a wide range of environment types (ViZDoom-Two-Color, T-Maze, four Atari games, three MuJoCo tasks in three dataset regimes), which is a reasonably broad evaluation surface.

The ablation studies are fairly extensive: curriculum learning effects, memory-token corruption/replacement experiments, number of segments, and memory size, providing some insight into what components matter.
The interpretability analysis via attention maps (read/write memory subsequences) is a nice qualitative addition that attempts to substantiate the claim that memory is actually used.
Code is made publicly available, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution is largely an engineering combination of an existing memory mechanism (RMT/Transformer-XL-style memory tokens) with an existing sequence-modeling RL framework (DT), plus a curriculum training recipe; there is little new architectural or algorithmic insight beyond this transplant.

The main memory-intensive benchmark results are not fully convincing: in T-Maze, even RATE-7 gradually degrades toward the 50% (random-guessing) success rate as the number of inference segments grows, indicating the memory mechanism does not robustly solve the long-horizon dependency task, only slows the failure mode compared to DT.

ViZDoom-Two-Color results show very high variance (e.g., 16.46 ± 6.90 vs DT90's 6.08 ± 1.62), and overlapping confidence intervals across some conditions raise doubts about the statistical significance of the reported gains.

In MuJoCo, RATE's benefits from memory tokens are explicitly described by the authors as "minimal," and RATE actually underperforms baselines (CQL, DT, or TAP) in several settings (e.g., Medium HalfCheetah, Medium-Replay Hopper), undermining the claim of consistent "better or comparable" performance.

The comparison protocol between RATE and DT is potentially confounded: RATE uses sequential sampling from the start of the trajectory plus curriculum learning, while DT uses random subsequence sampling; these training-procedure differences (not just the memory architecture) could account for much of the observed gap, but this is not carefully disentangled via matched-training-procedure ablations for DT.

The additional ablations (Appendix D) show inconsistent or even negative effects of scaling memory size or number of segments beyond 3, weakening the narrative that more memory capacity straightforwardly helps, and suggesting the mechanism's benefits are fairly narrow and environment-specific.

Curriculum learning requires a priori knowledge of the environment's episodic structure (e.g., trajectory length distribution) to construct increasing-length trajectory subsets, which limits the generality and practicality of the proposed training procedure for arbitrary offline RL settings.

Baselines used for comparison (DT, TAP, CQL) are comparatively dated; no comparison is made to other more recent memory-augmented transformer RL approaches (e.g., TrMRL, AdA-style models) that are discussed in the related work but never empirically benchmarked against.

Reported results rely on small sample sizes (e.g., 3 seeds for Atari/MuJoCo, 10 runs for T-Maze) without formal significance testing, which is a concern given the frequently overlapping error bars used to support the paper's central claims.

Presentation issues: some typographical/grammatical errors (e.g., "memory toxins" instead of "memory tokens") suggest insufficient proofreading, and several figures/tables are dense and not always clearly explained in the main text.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem: extending effective context in transformer-based offline RL via recurrent memory, which is important for memory-intensive decision-making tasks.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning memory-intensive environments (ViZDoom-Two-Color, T-Maze) as well as classic Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks, showing the method is broadly applicable and not just tuned for one setting.

Thoughtful ablation studies: effect of curriculum learning, number of segments, memory embedding size, and a 'RATE-' variant (segment training without memory) that isolates the contribution of the memory mechanism itself.

Interesting interpretability analysis using attention maps showing that memory tokens are actively read from and written to, and a targeted intervention experiment replacing memory tokens with noise/stale values, which strengthens the causal claim that memory is being used meaningfully.
Public code release supports reproducibility.
Qualitative case study (ViZDoom trajectory in Figure 3) nicely illustrates the practical consequence of forgetting vs. remembering, adding intuitive support beyond aggregate metrics.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core idea is largely a direct application of the existing Recurrent Memory Transformer (Bulatov et al., 2022) mechanism to the Decision Transformer framework, with relatively modest new architectural or algorithmic contributions beyond training procedure adaptations.

Missing comparisons to other relevant memory-augmented transformer baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., TrMRL, Working Memory Graph, Compressive Transformer, AdA-style Transformer-XL), leaving it unclear how RATE compares against alternative memory approaches rather than just vanilla DT.

Some results show large variance and inconsistent improvements: ViZDoom-Two-Color reward has very high standard error (16.46±6.90) which weakens the statistical confidence in the reported gains; several MuJoCo settings (e.g., Medium-Replay Hopper) show RATE underperforming DT/CQL/TAP.

On T-Maze, RATE's advantage is bounded (success rate still degrades to chance beyond roughly 3x the trained segment count), suggesting the memory mechanism does not generalize to substantially longer horizons than seen in training, somewhat limiting the claimed benefit for long-term dependency modeling.

The training procedures (e.g., curriculum learning scheme, starting all trajectories from the beginning) appear to require environment-specific knowledge and manual tuning, which may limit practical generality and reproducibility across new domains.

No analysis of computational cost/efficiency trade-offs (e.g., training time, memory footprint, wall-clock inference cost) versus a plain long-context DT baseline, despite motivating the work partly via the quadratic attention cost problem.

Minor clarity/writing issues (e.g., 'memory toxins' typo, some awkward phrasing) and the paper could better justify some design choices, such as why the specific curriculum and segment sampling strategies were chosen over alternatives (e.g., weighted loss).

strengths: Proposes a reasonably novel architecture (RATE) combining recurrent memory embeddings (RMT-style) with cached hidden states and a new Memory Retention Valve (MRV) gating mechanism to control memory updates in offline RL transformers.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning four memory-intensive environments (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid.Memory) plus standard Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks, demonstrating breadth of testing.
Thorough ablation study comparing five different MRV variants (cross-attention, gated, GRU, LSTM) with clear quantitative results showing the cross-attention variant is best.

Introduces a novel diagnostic environment (Action Associative Retrieval) specifically designed to more rigorously verify whether a model is actually using memory versus exploiting biases, which is a nice methodological contribution.

Clear qualitative and quantitative evidence (e.g., ViZDoom pillar color retention, T-Maze extrapolation to corridors far longer than training) that the proposed memory mechanism helps retain and use information beyond the context window, unlike the DT baseline.
Reports GPU memory/compute savings from segment-based training relative to DT with similar parameter counts, which is a practically relevant benefit.
weaknesses: Comparisons against DMamba and MambaDM in Tables 1-2 are taken directly from other papers rather than reproduced under a controlled, unified protocol (same seeds, dataset splits, hardware), which weakens the validity of head-to-head claims.

The only self-run baseline for memory-intensive environments is Decision Transformer; no comparison to other memory-augmented transformer RL approaches mentioned in related work (e.g., Transformer-XL-based agents, AMAGO, GTrXL/AdA-style architectures) despite these being directly relevant and discussed.

Results on standard benchmarks (Atari, MuJoCo) are mixed—RATE underperforms DT/other baselines in some cases (e.g., SeaQuest, MR HalfCheetah/Hopper), undercutting the claim of consistent 'universality' across task types.

Statistical rigor is limited: many experiments use only 3-6 runs with large error bars that sometimes overlap with baselines, making some superiority claims (e.g., Memory Maze results) less convincing.

The architecture introduces multiple additional hyperparameters (number of segments N, effective context, curriculum learning schedule, MRV configuration) that are tuned per-environment without a systematic sensitivity or robustness analysis, raising reproducibility and generalizability concerns.

No mention of code/checkpoint release specific to this submission, which combined with the many environment-specific custom modifications (e.g., modified ViZDoom-Two-Colors, custom T-Maze reward/observation) makes exact reproduction difficult.

The manuscript contains numerous grammatical errors and unclear phrasing (e.g., 'This proofs', 'in thein Table 3', awkward sentence constructions) that reduce clarity and polish expected at a top-tier venue.
The theoretical motivation for the specific MRV cross-attention design is not well justified beyond empirical ablation; a more principled analysis of why MRV-CA-2 outperforms alternatives is missing.
Some claims (e.g., 'RATE outperforms DT in 9/9 cases' for MuJoCo) are based on marginal differences within overlapping standard deviations, overstating the strength of the results.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely relevant problem: enabling transformer-based offline RL policies to exploit information beyond the attention context window via a recurrent memory mechanism.

The proposed MRV (cross-attention based memory update gate) is a reasonably clean architectural addition, and the paper includes a thorough ablation comparing five different MRV variants (CA-1, CA-2, gated, GRU, LSTM), showing that a specific configuration performs best.

The custom Action Associative Retrieval (AAR) environment is a nice diagnostic tool that isolates and quantifies whether a model is actually using out-of-context information, rather than merely benefiting from dataset bias.

Evaluation spans a reasonably broad set of environments (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid.Memory, Atari, MuJoCo), and hyperparameters/training details are reported in appendices, aiding reproducibility.
The component ablation (memory embeddings vs. cached hidden states vs. MRV) and curriculum learning study add some useful insight into what drives performance in T-Maze/Minigrid.Memory.
weaknesses: The only true memory-free baseline used throughout is vanilla Decision Transformer; there is no comparison against other memory-augmented transformer RL agents (e.g., GTrXL/TrXL-based PPO agents, AMAGO, or even the original Recurrent Memory Transformer applied to RL) which are the most directly relevant prior work and would better contextualize the claimed gains.

Technical novelty is limited: the architecture is essentially a combination of existing components (RMT's read/write memory tokens, Transformer-XL-style hidden-state caching, and a cross-attention gating block similar in spirit to GTrXL's gating), rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the paper does not clearly articulate what is conceptually new beyond this combination.

Most memory-intensive environments used (T-Maze, AAR, Minigrid.Memory, even ViZDoom-Two-Colors) are small, synthetic, low-dimensional tasks; there is no evaluation on larger-scale or more realistic long-horizon memory tasks (e.g., robotics manipulation with occlusion, or more complex 3D navigation) despite the paper's claim of relevance to robotics.

Results on Atari and MuJoCo (the 'versatility' claims) are weak evidence: differences from DT/Mamba baselines are often within one standard deviation, and since these tasks are explicitly stated not to require memory, the comparisons don't strongly support the paper's core contribution — they mostly show parity, not benefit.

Statistical rigor is limited: most experiments use only 3–6 runs with overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., Memory Maze results, several Atari/MuJoCo entries), making some of the claimed improvements only marginally supported.

The comparison protocol (RATE's effective context Keff vs. DT's context K) advantages RATE with additional forward-pass structure and recurrent computation across segments while claiming similar parameter counts; the fairness of this comparison in terms of compute/inference cost is not thoroughly analyzed beyond a brief GPU memory table.

The explanation for why the cross-attention MRV (CA-2) outperforms GRU/LSTM/gated alternatives is largely empirical/anecdotal, without deeper theoretical or mechanistic analysis of why this particular architecture retains information better.

Writing quality has rough edges (garbled sentences, minor typos such as 'thein Table 3', inconsistent notation), and some parts of the method description (e.g., exact segment-level masking scheme) require careful re-reading to fully understand, hurting clarity and reproducibility from the text alone.

The significance/impact of the contribution is unclear given that it mostly re-validates known findings (transformers without memory fail beyond their context window) rather than establishing a new capability or substantially advancing the state of the art relative to existing memory mechanisms in RL.

strengths: Extensive and diverse experimental evaluation spanning four dedicated memory-intensive environments (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid.Memory) as well as standard Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks, demonstrating the model's versatility across different observation types (image/vector), reward structures (sparse/dense), and action spaces (discrete/continuous).

The proposed Memory Retention Valve (MRV) is a reasonably novel contribution for offline RL, and the paper backs its design with a careful ablation comparing five different valve architectures (cross-attention variants, gating, GRU, LSTM), clearly justifying the chosen configuration with quantitative results (Table 3, Figure 8).

The custom-designed Action Associative Retrieval (AAR) environment is a nice methodological contribution that isolates and explicitly tests for memory usage via a formal correlation-based criterion, strengthening the claim that RATE genuinely retains and uses out-of-context information rather than exploiting spurious biases.

Thorough ablations addressing multiple design questions (component contributions, curriculum learning necessity, MRV configuration) give good insight into why and how the architecture works, going beyond simple performance tables.
Good reproducibility support: detailed appendices with environment descriptions, training procedures, hyperparameters, encoder architectures, and compute/parameter-count comparisons.

The comparison controlling for effective context length (Kef f for RATE vs. K for DT) is a sensible and fair experimental design choice that isolates the effect of the memory mechanism from mere context size.
weaknesses: The core architectural novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely recombines existing ideas (Recurrent Memory Transformer's memory tokens, Transformer-XL's cached hidden states, and a GTrXL-inspired gating/attention valve) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the main contribution is the application/adaptation to offline RL and the MRV valve design.

Despite extensive discussion of memory-augmented transformers in related work (RMT, Memformer, MART, Memorizing Transformer, GTrXL/AdA), none of these are used as direct empirical baselines — only vanilla DT and SSM-based models (DMamba, MambaDM) are compared, leaving open whether RATE's specific combination outperforms simpler memory-transformer adaptations to RL.

On the 'versatility' benchmarks (MuJoCo, Atari), RATE's advantage is inconsistent and often within standard-error overlap with SSM-based competitors (e.g., MuJoCo Medium and Medium-Replay results are frequently not top-1), so the claim of maintaining/improving classic-environment performance is only partially supported.

Some statistical reporting is thin: Memory Maze results are based on only 3 training runs, and several reported gains (e.g., in T-Maze ablations, ViZDoom) rely on modest numbers of seeds/runs without deeper significance testing.

Dataset generation for ViZDoom-Two-Colors involves a hand-crafted setup (agent always spawned facing the pillar, dataset collected from a differently-trained A2C policy) that may introduce confounds not fully controlled for or discussed.
The paper's writing contains some imprecise or informal statements (e.g., 'This proofs that DT-5 struggles') and could benefit from tighter editing for clarity and rigor.

The MRV ablation (Table 3) and the main results are all evaluated on relatively short/simple synthetic tasks (T-Maze, AAR) which, while illustrative, may not fully predict behavior on more complex, realistic long-horizon POMDP tasks beyond the four chosen memory environments.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem (memory in offline RL transformers for POMDPs) and combines existing memory mechanisms (RMT-style memory tokens, TrXL-style hidden state caching) with a novel Memory Retention Valve (MRV) gating module.

Extensive empirical evaluation across a diverse set of memory-intensive environments (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid-Memory) as well as standard benchmarks (Atari, MuJoCo), showing consistent improvements over DT and competitive/comparable performance to RMT, TrXL, and Mamba-based baselines.

Thorough ablation studies (RQ1-RQ3) probing which components (memory embeddings vs. cached hidden states) matter in which environment types, an OracleDT upper-bound analysis, and a systematic comparison of five different MRV architectures with clear justification for the chosen design (MRV-CA-2).

Interesting analysis of bias in training data (ViZDoom-Two-Colors red/green pillar experiment) and extrapolation to much longer sequences than seen during training (T-Maze up to 900 vs Kef f=90/150), demonstrating genuine benefits of the memory mechanism beyond simply fitting training distributions.

Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, training procedures, and additional custom benchmark (Action Associative Retrieval) to isolate and quantify memory usage with a principled mathematical criterion.
Additional technical efficiency comparison (GPU memory, training time) showing RATE requires less memory than DT for equivalent effective context, which is a practically relevant advantage.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core architecture largely combines existing techniques (RMT memory tokens + TrXL caching) with an added cross-attention gating module (MRV); the individual components (cross-attention retention) are conceptually similar to existing gating mechanisms in GTrXL and other memory transformer literature.

Baselines are described as "adapted" from NLP without much detail on how RMT and TrXL were adapted to the RL/offline setting, raising reproducibility concerns about whether comparisons are fully fair (e.g., same total parameter budget, tuning effort per baseline).

Improvements on non-memory-intensive benchmarks (Atari, MuJoCo) are relatively modest and mixed (RATE is not top-1 in many MuJoCo tasks, and SeaQuest results are worse than MambaDM), which somewhat weakens the claim of "universality."

The ablation for MRV configurations and hyperparameters is done primarily on T-Maze/ViZDoom-Two-Colors and may not generalize to other environments (e.g., Memory Maze, Minigrid-Memory), so the robustness of the specific MRV-CA-2 design choice across tasks is not fully established.

Statistical rigor is limited: many results are reported with small numbers of runs (Nruns as low as 3), and while sem/std are reported, no significance testing is performed to substantiate claims of RATE being significantly better than close competitors (e.g., TrXL, RMT) in several tables.

The paper's limitations section acknowledges that effective context design (choosing K and N) is ad hoc and not principled, and there's no study of the memory capacity of the model, which limits practical applicability and understanding of when RATE will succeed or fail.

The writing sometimes conflates different notions of "memory" (embeddings vs. cached states) with inconsistent attribution of which components matter for which environment, which could be clarified with a more unified theoretical framework rather than purely empirical observations.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning several memory-intensive environments (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid-Memory) as well as standard Atari/MuJoCo benchmarks, showing a genuine effort at broad coverage.

Thorough ablation studies (RQ1-RQ3) probing the role of memory embeddings vs. cached hidden states, an upper-bound OracleDT analysis, and a systematic comparison of five different MRV gating variants.

The custom Action Associative Retrieval (AAR) diagnostic and the noise-injection experiments provide some mechanistic insight into why DT fails on out-of-context information and how RATE's memory tokens carry it.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility material (algorithms, hyperparameter tables, training details in appendices).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution (MRV) is a fairly incremental combination of pre-existing memory mechanisms (RMT-style memory tokens, TrXL-style hidden-state caching) plus a cross-attention gate that is conceptually close to existing gating schemes (GTrXL, Memformer, MART); the novelty over prior memory-transformer literature is limited.

Comparisons across baselines are not fully controlled: DT is given full context K=Keff while RATE/RMT/TrXL use a much smaller per-segment K with recurrence; this asymmetry (plus disabling the feed-forward block only for RATE) muddies claims of a fair architectural comparison.

Results are mixed and often not decisive: on Minigrid-Memory RATE is beaten by TrXL on small grids and by RMT on large grids, with only a vague claim of being "better on average"; on MuJoCo, RATE's mean score (78.5) is actually lower than MambaDM (79.0) and DMamba (78.8), undercutting the paper's "universality" narrative.
Many reported improvements are within overlapping standard errors/deviations (e.g., several MuJoCo and Atari entries), so statistical significance of the claimed gains is unclear.

The memory-intensive environments used are custom/modified versions of existing benchmarks (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Minigrid-Memory), which complicates comparison with prior published results and raises reproducibility concerns despite appendix details.

No comparison to more recent/stronger memory-augmented or in-context RL baselines mentioned in the related work (e.g., AMAGO, Decision S4, GTrXL-based agents), leaving it unclear how RATE stacks up against the current state of the art rather than just DT/RMT/TrXL reimplementations.

The curriculum-learning experiment yields negligible or even slightly negative effects with limited explanation, and several design choices (MRV configuration, number of memory/cached tokens) appear to be selected via extensive per-environment grid search rather than principled design, raising concerns about overfitting to the specific benchmarks tested.

The paper's own limitations section acknowledges that context/segment sizing must be manually tuned to capture key events and that there is no analysis of the model's actual memory capacity, which are significant practical limitations for the claimed generality of the approach.

strengths: The paper combines several existing memory ideas (RMT-style memory tokens, TrXL-style hidden state caching, and a novel cross-attention-based Memory Retention Valve) into a coherent architecture (RATE) tailored to offline RL trajectory modeling.

Extensive experimentation across a wide variety of environments: four memory-intensive benchmarks (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid-Memory), plus standard Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks, showing the model is broadly competitive, not just on memory tasks.

Strong and thoughtful ablation studies (RQ1-RQ3): noise-injection experiments to localize where information is stored (memory embeddings vs cached hidden states), an OracleDT upper-bound comparison, and a systematic comparison of five different MRV variants (cross-attention, gating, GRU, LSTM) that clearly justifies the final design choice.

Interesting additional diagnostic environment (Action Associative Retrieval) and correlation-based analysis that provides a clean, quantitative way to demonstrate DT's failure to generalize beyond context length versus RATE's success.

Comparisons against a good range of baselines including transformer memory baselines (RMT, TrXL), recurrent baselines (LSTM, GRU), state-space baselines (Mamba variants), and non-memory baseline (DT), which contextualizes RATE's contribution against multiple types of related work.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed algorithms (Algorithm 1, 2), extensive hyperparameter tables, dataset collection methodology, and technical/compute details reported in the appendix.
weaknesses: Improvements on Atari and MuJoCo (the non-memory-intensive benchmarks) are often marginal and within/near standard deviation of competing methods (e.g., MambaDM), somewhat undercutting the 'universality' claim in the abstract/contributions since gains there are not clearly attributable to the memory mechanism.

The datasets for several memory-intensive environments (e.g., T-Maze, Minigrid-Memory) are generated by an oracle or a specialized PPO+TrXL policy rather than more standard/independent behavior policies, which could make the offline learning problem easier than realistic offline RL settings and raises some concern about how representative the results are of general offline RL performance.

The comparison design (K for RATE/RMT/TrXL vs. K=Keff for DT) somewhat confounds context-length and memory-mechanism effects; while the paper argues all models 'process the same parts of trajectories,' it is not fully clear this a fair apples-to-apples comparison in terms of e.g. number of attention operations or optimization dynamics.

Limited theoretical analysis of why the specific MRV-CA-2 configuration works best; the explanation is largely empirical/ablation-based rather than grounded in a principled argument, and the five candidate MRV designs feel somewhat ad hoc.

Some claims (e.g., 'significantly outperforms baselines,' 'demonstrates versatility') are strong relative to the more nuanced, mixed pattern of results seen across individual environments and tables, particularly in Minigrid-Memory where RATE is only 'on average' better rather than dominant.

The paper's stated limitations (inability to design K/N ensuring important events fall within effective context, no formal memory capacity analysis) are acknowledged but not empirically explored, leaving open questions about robustness/generality of the approach in less controlled settings.
